listening.title: Listening
listening.passage:
Interviewer: How do you communicate with your classmates when you are working on a project?
Salim: We usually use a group message, but we meet face to face when the project is difficult.
Interviewer: Do you use body language during presentations?
Salim: Yes. I try to make eye contact and use natural gestures.
Interviewer: What is the biggest problem with group messages?
Salim: Sometimes people read a message but do not reply. Then we do not know if they agree.
Interviewer: How are you solving that problem?
Salim: We are using a short online meeting every Sunday evening.

reading.passage: Students today have many ways to communicate. A class may use a message group to share reminders, but written messages do not always show tone clearly. A short sentence can sound unfriendly even when the writer does not intend it. Face-to-face conversation can solve this problem because speakers can use their voice, facial expressions and gestures. However, online communication is useful when students need to share a file quickly or contact a classmate who is not at school. The best choice depends on the purpose of the message.

Host: What changed when you became a teenager, Amal?
Amal: I became more independent. I started planning my own study time and helping at home.
Host: Do you still spend time with your friends?
Amal: Of course. Good friends support me when I feel worried.
Host: What happened last weekend?
Amal: I was studying when my friend called. We talked for twenty minutes and then I finished my homework.
Host: What advice would you give younger students?
Amal: Do not compare yourself with everyone online. Focus on your own goals.

reading.passage: Teenagers experience many changes as they grow older. They often want more independence, but they still need support from family and friends. A strong friendship is based on trust and respect. Friends can listen to a problem and offer advice, but they should not make every decision for each other. Social media can help friends stay in contact, yet it can also create pressure when teenagers compare their lives with carefully selected pictures online. Healthy friendships allow people to be themselves and to disagree politely.

Guide: Our visitors have three days in Oman. What should we include?
Mariam: On the first day, I suggest Nizwa Fort and the old market.
Guide: Good. What about the second day?
Mariam: We are going to travel to the desert and spend the night near the dunes.
Guide: And the final day?
Mariam: We will return through a mountain village. The scenery is spectacular.
Guide: How will the visitors travel?
Mariam: They are travelling in a small group by comfortable bus.

reading.passage: A small tour company designed a three-day trip for visitors who wanted to experience Omani culture and landscapes. On the first day, the group explored a historic fort and a traditional market. On the second day, they travelled towards the desert. They watched the sunset and stayed in comfortable tents. On the final day, the visitors drove through a mountain village and stopped to take photographs. The guide explained local traditions and reminded visitors to respect the environment. The group returned to Muscat in the evening.

Huda: The smart lighting system. It turns lights off automatically when nobody is in the room.

reading.passage: Online shopping makes it easy to compare products and order them from home. However, customers should read descriptions and terms carefully before paying. A product may look different from its photograph, or delivery may take longer than expected. Customers should keep the receipt and check the return policy. If an item arrives damaged, they should contact the company and explain the problem clearly. A reliable online store usually provides information about payment, delivery, guarantees and returns. Good online shoppers compare these details instead of choosing a product only because its price is low.
